strengths: The paper is well written and easy to follow.
Relational structures seem to provide a general unified framework that includes not only simplicial message passing but also other higher order structures.
Propositions and theorem are well defined and proofs are mathematically sound.
Strong theoretical contribution, establishing connections between different classes of GNNs.
Theoretical machinery for understanding over squashing and other phenomena in relational and topological GNNs
New rewiring heuristics for relational and topological GNNs
The paper successfully extends key results on graph oversquashing to topological domains, providing a comprehensive theoretical foundation for this adaptation.
The paper tackles questions that have been of interest to the TDL community, as highlighted in the recent position paper [1].

This paper addresses a critical gap in the literature on over-squashing. Over-squashing remains underexplored in the context of higher-order message-passing architectures like simplicial neural networks and CW networks. This paper takes an essential first step toward addressing this gap within Topological Deep Learning.
By presenting a unifying, axiomatic framework, a relational perspective on simplicial and cellular complexes is provided.
This unified approach facilitates the analysis of over-squashing in topological message-passing networks.
The message-passing theory of simple complexes and their relational structures is comprehensively and intensely studied, and a detailed explanation and rigorous proof are provided.
The article has a clear structure and a smooth and natural expression, which is easy for readers to understand and grasp.
weaknesses: The experimental settings where the combination of lifting and rewiring leads to performance improvements seems to be limited.
Minor room for improvement in the definition of the terminology; more explanations in natural language when defining terminology could make it a bit easier for the reader.
Limited real-world datasets used in the experiments.
Missing discussion of the complexity–accuracy trade-off by omitting a discussion of the computational complexity of the rewiring techniques.
Evaluation only on TUD dataset provides very limited empirical evidence for the method.
Lack of testing on node and link prediction problems.
Overall weak empirical evidence that the proposed method is helpful in practice and worth the overhead.

The novelty of the paper is somewhat limited; it reduces simplicial complexes to an "influence graph" and re-derives several previously established results on graph oversquashing, mirroring existing studies.

It remains unclear whether lifting graphs to higher-order domains could mitigate some effects of oversquashing; the paper does not address this question theoretically and its empirical analysis only begins to explore this comparison.
The paper quickly reduces simplicial message passing to a relational setting, which is more combinatorial than topological; it lacks analysis leveraging properties such as topological curvature.
The experimental section uses only outdated TUD benchmarks with few samples and problematic evaluation; newer benchmarks such as Zinc and OGB datasets should be included.
The experiments do not include cyclic lifting across all experiments, despite its use in recent TDL models like CIN and CIN++.
Effects of rewiring on real-world datasets appear inconclusive, making it difficult to determine when rewiring should be applied with TDL models.

The substitution of $R_i$ with $\mathcal{S}^{n_i}$ has minimal impact, diminishing the role of relations $R_i$ and treating all possible $n_i$-tuples as potentially related rather than focusing on specific relations.
The shift operator $A^{R_i}$ does not account for signal permutations, limiting the expressiveness of the relational structure.
The update rule and message functions appear to be a straightforward extension of prior work, lacking significant innovation or depth.
Literature review focuses on work up to 2020, lacking recent advancements in heterogeneous graphs and dynamic relational structures.
Insufficient SOTA comparison in the past two years; missing detailed comparison against recent models that address over-squashing with spectral techniques or adaptive message passing.
Failure to show results on deeper models; lacks experiments with varying numbers of message-passing layers to demonstrate effectiveness in mitigating over-squashing as depth increases.
No ablation experiments to verify impact of local complexity, model depth, and hidden dimension on performance.
Many formulas are not original and lack proper attribution/references.
Disproportionate amount of space devoted to simplicial complex background relative to solution description, leading to unbalanced impression.
